institution: monastery or math of the Sankeshvar Svāmi
what_is_said: Maṭh of about two acres, gate to the north, sacrifice hall (yajñamaṇṭap) for 1000 on the Kashmal Hiranikeshi; present svāmī 12th in succession. Devotees Brahmans, Rajputs, Marāṭhās, Shimpis, Panchals, Gabits; jurisdiction 'from the Malprabha to the Himalayas (?) and from the Nizam's territories to the Konkan coast'. Income c. Rs 30,000 a year from 30 inām villages (footnote: 15 in Kolhapur, 5 Belgaum, 3 Nizam's territory, 2 each Patvardhan estate, Satara, Savantvadi, 1 Bijapur) plus tribute and re-admission fines; feeds 10,000 Brahmans in Shrāvaṇ; svāmī usually on tour levying contributions. Local account: Shankarbharati, successor of Vishvarupacharya of Śṛṅgeri, left Śṛṅgeri c. 1570, was refused re-entry, founded Kudalgi, then (at Haridradevi's bidding, Vallabhgad) worshipped Shankarling at Sankeshvar; villages granted by Randulkhan (1569-1615, Bijapur officer) let him open maṭhs at Kolhapur and Sankeshvar; more villages from a Kolhapur chief c. 1670, additions till 1838.
quote: The monastery or math of the Sankeshvar Svd.mi is a large building about two acres in circumference. The chief gate faces north, and, by the south gate, flows a rivulet called the Kashmal Hiranikeshi. ' A sacrifice chamber or yajnamantap with room for- 1000 persons is built on the bank of the rivulet. The present svdmi is the twelfth in succession and was chosen by the late svdmi as his favourite disciple. The devotees of- the svdmi are Brahmans, Eajputs, Mardthds, Shimpis, Panchals, and Gabits, and his jurisdiction extends from the Malprabha to the Himalayas (?) and from the Nizam's territories to the Konkan coast. Besides tribute from disciples and re-admission fines paid by excommunicated followers, the monastery enjoys a- yearly revenue of about £3000 (Rs. 30,000) from thirty indm villages.
notes: Footnote notes neither Vishvarupacharya nor Shankarbharati is in Rice's Śṛṅgeri list. Same text in backup scan wbsl.17016. Also coded in sringeri/results/places.tsv P07.

institution: monastery opened by Shankarbharati with Bijapur grant
what_is_said: Villages granted by Randulkhan (1569-1615) "enabled the svāmi to open two more monasteries at Kolhapur and at Sankeshvar"; the Kolhapur house is thus presented as a foundation of the Sankeshvar line from the start.
quote: pleased with the svdmi's devotion that he granted him some villages which enabled the svdmi to open two more monasteries at Kolhd.pur and at Sankeshvar.
notes: Origin claim from the local account; compare RV04 (1959) which calls the Kolhapur maṭh the Karvir Pīṭha, separated c. 1909.

institution: math of the Sankeshvar Svāmi
what_is_said: Kolhapur city has two large maṭhs, one belonging to the Sankeshvar Svāmi and the other to a Jain Svāmi. No further detail.
quote: Besides these temples Kolhdépur has two large monasteries or maths, one belonging to the Sankeshvar Svdmi and the other to a Jain Svami.
notes: Also P09 in sringeri places.tsv.

institution: Ambabai (Mahalakshmi) temple: spire and domes
what_is_said: Spire and domes of the Ambābāī temple said to have been added by a Shankarācārya of Sankeshvar; the upper works said to have cost about Rs 1 lakh (£10,000). Jains claim the temple was originally a Padmavati temple and the spire and domes Brahmanic additions; the gazetteer agrees on architectural grounds.
quote: The spire and domes of this temple are said to have been added by a Shankardchdérya of Sankeshvar; the Jains declare that the temple
notes: Second statement on p.310: "The upper works added by Shankaracharya are said to have cost about £10,000 (Rs. 1 lakh)".

institution: inām village
what_is_said: Khidrapur, "an alienated village belonging to Sankeshvar Svāmi", population 1036 (1881), on the Krishna 12 miles SE of Shirol; entry otherwise describes the Kopeshvar temple.
quote: Khidra’pur, an alienated village ®elonging to Sankeshvar Svémi, wth in 1881 a population of 1036, lies on the Krishna
notes: RV04 (1959) Khidrapur entry (p.847) drops the clause about the Svāmi.

institution: Ambabai temple: spire and domes
what_is_said: Reprint of the 1886 statement that the spire and domes were added by a Śaṅkarācārya of Saṅkeśvar.
quote: The spire and domes of this temple are said to have been added by a Sahkara- carya of Sahke^var ; the Jains declare
notes: Reprints the 1886 text (with "Sahkara- carya of Sahke^var"); the clause on Rs 1 lakh cost not checked.

institution: Shankaracharya Math or Karvir Pīṭha
what_is_said: Old plain two-storeyed building in Shukravar Peth on the way to the Panchganga ghat, "occupied by Sankaracarya of Sankesvar"; formerly part of the Saṅkeśvar Maṭh, the link "was broken about 50 years ago" (c. 1909) and the Kolhapur maṭh is now known as the Karvir Pīṭha. Index: "Shankaracharya Math or Karvir Peeth, 874".
quote: Sankardcdrya Math. — This mafh is in Sukravar Peth on the way to the Pancaganga Ghat. It is an old two storeyed structure without any embellishments or architectural points. It is, however, very old. The building is occupied by Sankaracarya of Sankesvar. Although formerly it was a part of the Sankesvar Math, the link was broken about 50 years ago and now the Kolhapur math is known as Karvir Pifha.
notes: New text, not in 1886 (1886 only: maṭh of the Sankeshvar Svāmi, p.312). Internal tension: still "occupied by Sankaracarya of Sankesvar" yet separate. Also P17 in sringeri places.tsv.

institution: math of Dr Kurtakoti, Shankaracharya of Karveer
what_is_said: Dr Kurtakoti, "the Shankaracharya of Karveer", took part in 1928 in converting Miss Miller, an American Christian, to Hinduism (renamed Sharmishtha, later married Tukojirao Holkar); he "made Nasik his residence for a number of years" and spread social and religious reform "from his math at Panchavati".
quote: Dr. Kiirtakoli (Shankaracharya of Karaveer) made Nasik his re.sidence for a number of years and his influence spread widely in favour of religious and social reform from his math at Panchavati.
notes: New text (not in 1883). Conversion passage p.199: "Dr. Kurtkoti, the Shankaracharya of Karveer, actively participated in converting Miss Miller". Whether his Panchavati maṭh is the old Shankaracharya monastery (W-row Nasik) is not said.

place: Kudalgi (Kudali), at the meeting of the Tunga and Bhadra
institution: monastery founded by Shankarbharati
what_is_said: In the Sankeshvar foundation story: Shankarbharati, refused re-entry at Śṛṅgeri, "started a monastery at Kudalgi" and put his newly chosen head in it with several villages he had acquired in the Nizam's territories; Kudalgi placed "about thirty miles south of Harihar".
quote: He started a monastery at Kudalgi and established his new head in it putting him in possession of several villages ,he had acquired in the Nizam
notes: Kudali is thus presented as a sibling of Saṅkeśvar from the same split (c. 1570).

institution: temple of Rangnath; village granted to the Kudalgi Svāmi
what_is_said: Old Rangnath temple at Hallur ruined by Tipu (1782-1799); the present building was made by the Svāmi of Kudalgi, to whom the village was granted by Hanmant Gaud, a chief of Havnur. Village of 654 people on the Tungabhadra c. 18 miles SE of Kod.
quote: Tho old temple of Rangnéth was ruined by Tipu Sultan (1782-1799) ; the present building was made by the Svdmi of Kudalgi to whom the village was granted by Hanmant Gaud a chief of Hévnur.
notes: Temple rebuilt by the Svāmi: link could also be "temple". Same text in dli.csl.3218 and gazetteerbombay12enthgoog. Not reprinted in RV03 (1959).

institution: procession privilege of the Kudalgi Svāmi
what_is_said: The Smārta Shankar Bharati Svāmi of Kudalgi "from time immemorial" has had the privilege of riding in a palkhi carried crossways through the streets (of Hubli); when the Liṅgāyat Mursavirad Svāmi imitated this c. 50 years earlier, the Smārta teacher sued; the court held there was no objection, upheld by the Sadar Adalat and the Privy Council.
quote: From time immemorial the Smart Shankar Bharati Svémi of Kudalgr in Maisur has enjoyed the privilege of riding in a palkhi or open litter carried crossways through tho public streets.
notes: Implies regular visits to Hubli; litigation date c. 1830s. Not reprinted in RV03.

institution: Shārada Pīṭh (Dwarka seat of the Shankaracharya)
what_is_said: Shankara founded four seats (Badri-Kedar, Rameshvar, Puri, Dwarka); "The Dwarka seat is called Shārada Pīth, Throne of Learning, and is endowed by the Gaekwar of Baroda, who sanctions the appointment of every new pontiff." Each pontiff has a territorial area; the Dwarka Shankaracharya is referee in religious questions for Shaivas in Gujarat.
quote: The Dwiirka seat is called Shdrada Pith Throne of Learning, and is endowed by the G&ekwar of Baroda, who sanctions the appointment of every new pontiff. The chief duty of the pontiff is to preach and disseminate the doctrines of the Yedic religion, to control the body of friars or Sdayasis, and generally to supervise the seat. AT certain territorial area is assigned to each pontiff, outside which he has no jurisdiction. The Dwarka pontiff, called Shankaracharya^ is a referee in religions questions for followers of Shaivism in Gujarat.
notes: Only Dvārkā maṭha passage found in the Gujarat volumes. Gives Rameshvar (not Śṛṅgeri) as the southern seat. Same text in backup in.ernet.dli.2015.281420. Kathiawar VIII (1884) Dwarka entry (p.~600, line 49640ff.) describes only the Dwarkanath temple and pilgrim fees: no maṭha.

institution: Shankaracharya tomb, Shiv temple and three-storied monastery
what_is_said: Enclosure with the tomb of a Shankaracharya "or Shaiv pontiff", a Shiv temple and a large three-storied monastery for Shaiv ascetics. Sachchidanand Shankaracharya "said to have come from Shringeri" under the second Peshwa (1720-40), died at Nasik after choosing Brahmanand, who died within a month; both buried there. Tombs and temple built by Savai Madhavrao (1774), rest-house by Nana Fadnis, monastery by Narushankar (1750); cost Rs 16,000; allowance Rs 500 from Pimpalner revenues and Government grant Rs 288 a year. Population chapter (p.42): Dravid Brahmans are connected with "the monastery of the great Shankaracharya" built in Panchavati by Nana Fadnavis, managed by a Dravid Brahman.
quote: a tomb of a Shankaracharya or Shaiv pontiff, and a temple of Shiv with wooden pillars on the north and some fine stone masonry in the south. At the back of the enclosure is a large three-storied monastery for Shaiv ascetics. In the time of the second Peshwa (1720-1740) Sachcliidanand Shankaracharya is said to have come from Shringeri in Maisur
notes: A short-lived independent pontificate of Śṛṅgeri origin; coded as unnamed because the text names no continuing seat. p.42 quote: "Dravius are connected with the monastery of the great Shankara- charya which was built in Panchavati by Ndna Fadntvis". Also P08 in sringeri places.tsv.

institution: Shankaracharya monastery and tombs
what_is_said: Reprint of the 1883 entry (tombs of Sachchidanand and Brahmanand, monastery by Naro Shankar, Rs 16,000) with an addition: "A fine bust of Shankaracharya has been installed on the tomb"; Government grant and Pimpalner allowance still mentioned without figures. People chapter (p.235) repeats the Dravida Brahmans' link to the monastery built by Nana Phadnavis.
quote: The toi.i cost is estimated at Rs. 16,000. A fine bust of Shankaracharya has bi.'c 1 installed on the tomb.
notes: Reprints colonial text, with the bust as the only new fact.

institution: great temple of Shankaracharya Svāmi; reputed burial place of a Shankaracharya
what_is_said: Nirmal is said to be the burial place of one of the great Shankaracharyas; on his death anniversary (Kartik vadya 11) a week-long fair draws 6000-7000 pilgrims (Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Parsis), trade c. Rs 10,000. Eight temples built c. 1750 by Shankarji Keshav (Phadke), Sarsubhedar of Bassein, after the fall of Bassein (1739); Shankaracharya Svāmi's temple has a Government grant of Rs 421 a year and is managed by a committee. Sopara entry (p.325) calls it "the great temple of Shankaracharya Svami" raised to mark the restoration of the old faith.
quote: being, according to tradition, the burying place of one of the great Shankar4cb4ryas, the apostles of the modern Brdhmanic system.
notes: Footnote: the great Shankaracharya died in Kashmir, so "This Nirmal Shankaracharya may have been one of his religious descendants". No maṭha or seat described. Also P12 in sringeri places.tsv.

institution: (no maṭha) meeting of the Shankaracharya and the Jain high priest
what_is_said: About 1750 the Jain Jati and "Shankaracharya the Brahmanical pontiff" met in Poona; after discussion it was agreed, "it is said by bribing the Shankaracharya", that a Jain temple could be built in a quarter where Brahmans did not live; the Peshwas granted the site.
quote: About 1750 the Jati or high priest of the Jatns and Shankaracharya the Br&hmanical pontiff happened to meet in Poona. After a long discussion it was,agreed, it is said by bribing the Shankaracharya
notes: Seat not named. Also P13 in sringeri places.tsv.

institution: existing religious pitha disestablished under Shahu Chhatrapati
what_is_said: Under Shahu, the existing religious pīṭha, which had enjoyed revenue from State endowments, "was practically disestablished and its endowments withdrawn".
quote: The existing religious pitha or organized religious centres which had proved itself to be incapable of a dynamic approach to its responsibilities and which had enjoyed revenues from State endowments was practically disestablished and its endowments withdrawn.
notes: The pīṭha is not named; probably the Śaṅkarācārya maṭh at Kolhapur (Karvir/Saṅkeśvar), which fits the c. 1909 break reported on p.874. Not in the 1886 text.

institution: residence of Bhāskarācārya, delegate of the Shankaracharya for the Komtis
what_is_said: Komtis' spiritual guide is the Shankaracharya, "to whom and to whose delegate, a Smart Brahman whose title is Bhaskaracharya, they give presents"; the present Bhāskarācārya, Arunachal Svāmi, lives at Narayan-Devarkeri in Bellary, is married, tours, and punishes Komti caste offences by fine or excommunication.
quote: whose delegate, a Smart Bréhman whose title is Bhdskardcharya, they give presents. ‘lhe present Bhdskardchdrya is Arundchal Svami who lives at Nardyan- Devarkori in Belléri.
notes: seat=other: Bhāskarācārya (Komati caste guru) as deputy of an unnamed Śaṅkarācārya.

place: Bodhan; Nander; near Hampi; near Pendgaon Pattan (Penukonda)
institution: four monasteries of Bhāskarācārya, deputy of the Shankaracharya
what_is_said: Komtis refer important questions to Bhāskarācārya, a Yajurvedi Apastambh Brahman, "the deputy of Shankaracharya", who has four monasteries: at Bodhan and Nander in the Nizam's country, near Hampi (36 miles NW of Bellary), and near Pendgaon Pattan in Mysore; he occasionally visits Sholapur; fines go to him.
quote: Bhaskar^ch^rya a lajurvedi Apastambh Brahman the deputy of ShankarAchfirya. He has four monasteries at Bodhan and Nander
notes: Four places in one row (one institution). Hampi link suggests the Virūpākṣa line, but the text does not say so.

institution: monastery of the Smārta svāmī of the Shenvis (Kavaḷe maṭha)
what_is_said: Smārta Shenvis are under a separate sannyāsī head; "The Smart svami has a monastery at Khanapur where he occasionally lives", endowed with the two villages of Mansapur and Lakudvadi; footnote: the Smārta svāmī generally lives at Sonavda in Kanara.
quote: The Smdrt svdmi has a monastery at Khanapur' where he occasionally lives, and which enjoys a grant of the two villages of Mansapur and Lakudvidi.
notes: seat=other: the Sārasvat Smārta (Kavaḷe/Gauḍapādācārya) maṭha; identification is mine. Advaita, but not one of the Śaṅkara pīṭhas.

institution: rich maths of the Shenvi svāmīs
what_is_said: Shenvis have two svāmīs, a Smārta living at Sonavda in Kanara and a Vaiṣṇava in Goa; "They have rich monasteries, maths, in Khanapur, Karwar, Bombay, Nasik, and Benares."
quote: They have two head priests, svdmis, one Smd/rt liviag in Sonavda in Kd,nara, and the other Vaishnav living in Goa. They have rich monasteries, maths, in Khdndpur, Karwdr, Bombay, Ndsik, and Benares.
notes: The text does not say which of the two svāmīs owns each maṭh. seat=other (Kavaḷe line). Same text in dli.csl.3335.

institution: Shenvi monastery with the tomb of Purnanand
what_is_said: Monastery about 175 years old, built in honour of Purnanand, a Shenvi ascetic and high priest whose tomb it contains; now the property of Atmanand Svāmi, present high priest of the Shenvis, with headquarters at Kavla in Goa, who occasionally visits Nasik; Peshwa allowance about Rs 300 a year; hereditary local manager a Yajurvedi Brahman paid about one third.
quote: In Nasik they have a monastery about I 75 years old, built in honour of Purnfinand a Shenvi ascetic and high priest of the caste whose tomb it contains. The monastery is now the property of Atmanand Svami, the present high priest of the Shenvi caste, whose head-quarters are at Kavla in Goa and who occasionally visits Nasik. The Peshwas granted it a yearly allowance of about £30 (Rs. 300).
notes: seat=other: Kavaḷe maṭha (Gauḍapādācārya) of the Smārta Sārasvats.

institution: Honalli (Svarṇavallī) Smārta math
what_is_said: Headquarters of the guru of the Havig Brahmans; 45th head, a minor of 11, affairs run by a manager under leading Havigs. Income from caste fines, temple lands and subscriptions of Havigs of Sirsi, Supa, Yellapur, Siddapur, Ankola and Sherogars; daily worship of Narsimh, Chandramauleshvar, Kashivishveshvar, Sharada, Ganpati and Shankaracharya; car festival (Vaishakh) with 3000-5000 people. Local history: Gunanidhi was made a sannyāsī (Vishvavandya Sarasvati) by "the famous Shankaracharya" at Benares; 18 teachers at Ujjain, then Gokarn and Kadtoka; the 29th settled at Sonda at the Sonda chief's invitation and was given a monastery and land; Arsappa Naik (1555-98) built temples and a monastery.
quote: The® Honalli or Smart monastery is the head-quarters of the spiritual ‘Teacher or guru of the Havig or Haig Bréhmans.
notes: seat=other (Svarṇavallī). Claims direct Śaṅkarācārya origin. Also P11 in sringeri places.tsv. Kanara XV-1 caste lines name it as "the Smart monastery of Honnalli at Sonda in Sirsi" (counted below).

institution: Smārta monastery at Kundal
what_is_said: Tiglers' religious guide "is the head of the Smart monastery at Kundal in Supa". No other detail.
quote: Their religious guide is the head of the Smdrt monastery at Kundal in Supa.
notes: Only mention found of a Smārta maṭh at Kundal (village by the Kundal pass, 22 miles SW of Supa); not in the Kanara XV-2 Places chapter. Could be an OCR or source slip.

institution: Jyotir-math, one of Śaṅkara's four maṭhs
what_is_said: Life of Śaṅkara: born at Kallady in Travancore, a Nambūri; founded maṭhs for his disciples at Sringeri (south), the Jyotir-math 'vulgo Joshimath' near Badrinath (north), the Śāradā-math at Dvārakā (west) and the Vardhana-math at Puri (east); late in life visited Kashmir, then Badari where he restored the ruined temples of Nārāyaṇ, and died at Kedār aged 32. Four principal disciples whose pupils head the Daśanāmī Daṇḍins.
quote: He made converts from every sect and class and established maths or monasteries for his disciples~the Sringeri-math on the Tungabhadia in Mysore to the south : the Jyotir-math (vulgo Joshi-~ math) near Badarinéth to the north
notes: Textbook four-maṭh statement; nothing on the maṭh's present state (no head, no buildings, not said to be living or vacant). The Joshimath entry in the same author's vol. III (AT12 p. 372-373) does not mention any maṭh.

place: Badrinath (with Joshimath as the Rawal's base)
institution: Badrinath temple and its Rawal (chief priest), linked to Śaṅkara
what_is_said: History chapter (p. 466): Śaṅkara displaced the Buddhist priests of Nārāyaṇa at Badrinath (and of Paśupati at Kedār) and brought in priests from the Dakhin 'whose successors still manage the affairs of those temples'. p. 783: legend that Śaṅkara on his digvijaya found the idols in the Nārada-kuṇḍ and re-established Viṣṇu worship at Badari. p. 787: 'some century and a half ago' (c. 1730s) the worship at Badrinath was conducted by Daṇḍi Paramahaṃsa fakirs from the Dakhin, who gave way to Nambūri ('Lanbiri') Brahmans from Malabar; three or four aspirants to the office of Rawal are always present, one officiating at Badrinath, the rest residing at Joshimath.
quote: Some century and a half ago the worship of Vishnu at Badrinath was conducted by Dandi Paramahansa fakirs from the Dakhin, but these gave way to Dakhini Brahmans of the Lanbiri caste from Kirat Malwaér. There are always three or four aspirants for the office of Rawal, as the chief priest is called, in attendance, one of whom usually takes the duty at Badrinath whilst the remainder reside at Joshimath
notes: Rawal's link to Śaṅkara is given as tradition (Dakhini priests installed by Śaṅkara). The Daṇḍi Paramahaṃsa predecessors are the closest the text comes to a Daśanāmī/Jyotirmaṭh presence; no Śaṅkarācārya of Joshimath is mentioned. Not a maṭh-head: the Rawal is a temple priest.

institution: tradition of Śaṅkarācārya at the Katyūrī capital
what_is_said: The Katyūrī kings first ruled from Joshimath; the temple of Basdeo (Vāsudeva) there is the oldest, Vāsudeva being 'the name given by Sankara' to the supreme being; the Katyūrīs aided Śaṅkara's reforms. One story makes Śaṅkarācārya the unwelcome visitor to the Rani at Joshimath, which the author reads as religious quarrels forcing the dynasty to leave Joshimath for Katyūr.
quote: Another story makes Sankardécharya the unwelcome visitor to the Rani whilst her husband Basdeo was engaged in his ablations at Vishnuprayag. Stripped of its embellishments the story would seem to show that the descendants of Basdeo were obliged to abandon Joshimath owing to religious quarrels
notes: No maṭh mentioned; a Śaṅkara tradition at Joshimath only.

institution: Vardhana-math, one of Śaṅkara's four maṭhs
what_is_said: In the four-maṭh list: 'the Vardhana-math at Puri in Orissa to the east'. Nothing else on the Puri maṭh.
quote: the Jyotir-math (vulgo Joshi-~ math) near Badarinéth to the north: the Sirada-math at Dwa- raka to the west and the Vardhana-math at Puri in Orissa to the east
notes: Same passage as the Jyotir-math row; coded separately because it locates the Govardhana seat.

institution: Daśanāmī Gosāins of Garhwal under the Sringeri maṭh
what_is_said: Gosāins founded by Śaṅkara are a powerful body in the hills; ruled by the Dasnāma assembly; 'The chief math of the order represented in Garhwal is at Sringeri'; they serve at Rudrnāth, Kalpeswar, Kamaleswar, Bhil-kedār and most of the principal Śiva temples.
quote: The chief math of the order repre- sented in GarhwAl is at Sringeri on the Tungabhadra river in the Madras Presidency
notes: Significant for Jyotirmath: in Garhwal itself the Daśanāmīs' chief maṭh is named as Sringeri, not Joshimath. Conflicts with AT12 p. 272 table, which assigns the northern Daśanāmīs (Giri, Parvata, Sāgara) to Joshimath.

what_is_said: Same table: Eastern division, chief math 'Bhog Gobardhan', system Bhogbar, affixes Ban, Aranya, holy tract Purushottama Puri or Jagannath, deity Jagannath, goddess Vimala, Ācārya Hastāmalaka, pilgrimage Mahodadhi, Rig Veda.

place: Badrinath (with Joshimath as the Rawal's base)
institution: Badrinath temple built by Śaṅkara; Nambūri Rawal
what_is_said: The temple 'said to have been erected some 800 years ago by Sankara Acharya'. Principal priests are Nambūri Brahmans from Malabar; the head priest is the Rawal; a chela of his caste always waits at Joshimath as Rawal-elect. The Rawal has an establishment and under the former Rajas had uncontrolled authority in the temple villages. Offerings c. Rs 5,000 in ordinary years. Joshimath entry (p. 372-373): residences of the Rawal and Badrinath priests, who winter there; no maṭh mentioned.
quote: The principal priests are Namburi Brahmans from Malabar and the head-priest is called Rawal. In order to provide for the succession, in ease of the illness or death of the Rawal, a chela of his caste is always in attendance at Joshimath, so that there is al- ways a Rawal elect present to take possession of the office.
notes: Śaṅkara-Rawal link is implicit (Śaṅkara built the temple; Malabar priests). The Joshimath entry (p. 372-373) is silent on any Śaṅkara maṭh or pīṭha.

institution: Badrinath temple at Dwarahat under the Rawal of Badrinath
what_is_said: At Dwarahat 'all the principal temples are ascribed to Sankaracharya'; the principal temple is dedicated to Badrinath; a footnote says it is 'under the Rawal of Badri'.
quote: From Dwéra, westward, all the principal temples are ascribed to Sankarachirya, and those here form no ex-
notes: Temple ascription to Śaṅkara plus subordination to the Badrinath Rawal; no maṭh. Coded because it ties a Kumaon temple to the Badrinath establishment. Footnote OCR garbled ('This is under the Rawal of Badri i P').

institution: temples at Joshimath and Badrinath founded by Śaṅkara
what_is_said: Śaṅkara purged Kumaon of degraded Buddhism and 're-established the famous temples at Kedarnath, Badrinath and Joshimath'; Viṣṇu worship 're-established in the hills by Sankara Acharya, who founded a temple at Joshimath to Vishnu under the name of Basdeo or Vasudeo, and another at Badrinath'.
quote: His worship was re-established in the hills by Sankara Aeharya, who founded a templo at Joshimath to Vishnu under the name of Basdeo or Vasudeo, and another at Badrinath.
notes: Śaṅkara's foundation at Joshimath is a temple, not a maṭh; the Jyotirmaṭh itself is not named. Almora volume, place in Garhwal.

institution: Badrinath temple at Dwarahat controlled by the Rawal of Badrinath
what_is_said: All the principal temples from Dwarahat westward are ascribed to Śaṅkarācārya; the principal Badrinath temple 'is connected with the greater institution in Garhwal of this name, and is controlled by the Rawal of that place'.
quote: From Dwarahat westward, all the principal temples are ascribed to Sankara A chary a and those here form no exception. The principal temple dedicat¬ ed to Badrinath is connected with the greater institution in Garhwal of this name, and is controlled by the Rawal of that place.
notes: Copies AT12 p. 222 with the footnote brought into the text. RV10 Almora (1981, s.v. Dwarahat) keeps the temple but drops both the Śaṅkara ascription and the Rawal.

institution: the Joshimath monastery founded by Śaṅkara
what_is_said: Śaivism, superseded by Buddhism, owes its restoration to Śaṅkara (fl. c. 7th-8th c.); he introduced Vāsudeva worship, insisted on the Himalayan pilgrimage, 'established the Joshimath monastery and restored the temple at Badrinath, finally proceeding to Kedarnath, where he died at the age of thirty-two'. Pilgrims 50,000-60,000 a year.
quote: He it was too, who insisted upon the efficacy of the pilgrimage to the holy places of the Himalayas. Ho established tho Joshimath monastery and restored the temple at Badriuath, finally proceeding to Kedarnath, where ho died at the age of thirty-two.
notes: The only colonial passage in the north set that names a Joshimath maṭh founded by Śaṅkara outside a four-maṭh list. Said nothing about its present state: the Joshimath entry (p. 168-170) describes the town as winter quarters of the Badrinath Rawal, temples of Narasiṃha, Vishnu etc., and is silent on any maṭh, Śaṅkarācārya or pīṭha (implicitly not a living seat).

institution: Badrinath temple built by Śaṅkara; Nambūri Rawal; estates
what_is_said: Original building 'said to have been erected by Sankara Acharya about the eighth century'. Treasure taken down to Joshimath, the winter headquarters. Endowment: in Almora 45 whole and 26 part villages, gunth revenue Rs 1,750; in Garhwal 164 whole villages and portions of 111 others, Rs 5,429. Rawal chose his successor (Lushington 1846) and received a sanad; 1893 the old Rawal abdicated temporal control; after an 1896 suit (s. 539 CPC) the secular management rests with the Rawal under the Raja of Tehri-Garhwal; the Rawal 'must be a Namburi Brahman from southern India'.
quote: The original building is said to have been erected by Sankara Acharya about the eighth century.
notes: Second quote for the Rawal: 'The Rawal must be a Namburi Brahman from southern Indinj, and a member of the priestly class of his clan' (p. 146). Śaṅkara link only via the temple's foundation; Joshimath as the Rawal's winter seat (p. 168).

institution: Sankaracharya math (= Govardhana maṭha, not so named)
what_is_said: Among the maṭhs clustered round Swarga-dwāra the Kabirpanthi and Śaṅkarācārya maṭhs are prominent; 'the latter math is said to have been founded by Sankaracharya himself', is evidently old (sand dunes all round), and has a fine library of about 1,200 manuscripts, some 300-400 years old. p. 112: over 70 maṭhs in Puri; the chief Śaiva maṭhs in the sandy tract near Swarga-dwār are Śaṅkarācārya, 'with a fine library of old manuscripts', and Sankarananda (branch at Bhubaneswar). p. 97: 'the learned pandit of the Sankaracharya monastery seeking salvation by the way of spiritual knowledge'.
quote: The latter math is said to have been founded by Sankaraoharya himself, and is evidently of considerable age, as the sand, barely kept back by cactus fences, rises all round into a high dune. It has a fine library containing about 1,200 manuscripts, of which some are 300 to 400 years old.
notes: Name 'Govardhana' not used. Hit file dli.ministry.07422 is a partial scan; quote and pages from the full scan in.ernet.dli.2015.206884. Sankarananda maṭh (Śaiva, branch at Bhubaneswar) not coded: no Śaṅkara link stated (RV29 App. III lists it as Dandi Sannyasi). Hunter's Puri (HU19, 1877) has no Śaṅkara maṭh: only unnamed 'little monasteries' at Swarga-dwāra (p. 66).

institution: Gobardhana (Bhogavardhana) Matha, the Sankaracharya Matha
chapter: Places (s.v. Puri: Mathas); also People, Education
what_is_said: Mathas section: 'Gobardhana Matha is one of the oldest in Puri and is believed to have been founded by Adi Sankaracharya in the 9th century'; Gobardhana and Sankarananda are the Śaiva maṭhs near Swargadwara; formerly temple priests were trained at the Sankaracharya Matha and needed its certificate to serve in the Jagannath temple, a function now performed by the Muktimandap (p. 811). p. 774: Sankaracharya Matha prominent at Swargadwara, 'said to have been founded by Sankaracharya'. p. 796: Śaṅkara (788-820) founded the 'Bhogavardhana or Gobardhana Matha at Puri which exists till to[day]'. p. 125: 'He established one of his four Mathas at Puri which still exists.' p. 475, 511: founded the Gobardhana matha 'which is still extant'; Puri's Sanskrit learning traced to him. p. 520: Śrīdhara Svāmin (14th c.) was Mahanta of the 'Govardhana pitha, a famous Sankarite moastery at Puri'. App. III (p. ~844): 'Sankaracharya or Bhogabardhan', Dandi Sannyasi.
quote: Gobardhana Matha is one of the oldest in Puri and is believed to have been founded by Adi Sankaracharya in the 9th century A. D.
notes: Places text at p. 774 reprints BG39 p. 288 (Kabirpanthi and Sankaracharya maṭhs at Swargadwara, Haridasa's grave) but drops the 1,200-MS library. New in 1977: the name Gobardhana/Bhogavardhana, its living status ('still extant'), the Śrīdhara tradition, and the former role in certifying Jagannath priests (now the Muktimaṇḍapa's). No Śaṅkarācārya (head) is named.

institution: Adi Sankar Pravupada Ashram (Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi foundation)
what_is_said: Foundation stone laid 3 March 1973 'at the instance of Shri Jagadguru of Kanchi Kamakoti Peetha'; three temples (Caitanya; Ādi Śaṅkara and his four disciples; Jayadeva with Padmāvatī and Bālakṛṣṇa); managed by the Sankar Bhagavadpada Seva Samiti with liberal donations from the Kāmakoṭi Pīṭha (Rs 1,70,000 for temples and Ashram). 1974-75: 7 boys aged 9-14 taught Sanskrit and the Paippalāda śākhā of the Atharvaveda by 1 full-time and 3 part-time teachers; 7-year course; library.
quote: At the instance of Sbri Jagadguru of Kanchi Kamakoti Peetha, Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu, the foundation stone of the Adi Sankar Pravupada Ashram, Puri, was laid on the 3rd March, 1973.
notes: Post-colonial; no colonial antecedent. A Kāñcī institution at the seat-town of Govardhana; the text does not relate it to the Gobardhana Matha.

institution: Sankar Math (founded 1919) and Sankaracharya Chatuspathi
what_is_said: 'The other attraction of Ramrajatala is the Sankar Math near the Ramrajatala railway station founded in 1326 B.S. (A.D. 1919) and named after Jagatguru Sri Sri Sankaracharyya.' p. 465: the Ramrajatala Sankaracharya Chatuspathi is one of the Sanskrit tols recognised by the Vangiya Sanskrit (Shiksha Parishad).
quote: The other attraction of Ramrajatala is the Sankar Math near the Ramrajatala railway station founded in 1326 B.S. (A.D. 1919) and named after Jagatguru Sri Sri Sankaracharyya.
notes: seat=other: a 20th-century maṭh named after Śaṅkara; no affiliation to any of the four seats stated. Not in colonial Howrah texts checked.

institution: Tarakeswar Math (Daśanāmī), held by court to be of the Śaṅkarācārya school
what_is_said: Quoting a court finding: the Daśanāmīs are Vedic Sannyasis, 'the Tarakeswar Math is governed by the Sankaracharya school of thought', and its Mohunt is a Mathadhari Daśanāmī Sannyasi (p. 209). Almost all Daśanāmī maṭhs in Bengal founded by Brahmans from the North-West. p. 726: Mayagiri Dhumrapan appointed Mohanta (1729); subsidiary seats at Guptipara, Nayangarh Bhot-bagan, Baidyabati, Garh Bhavanipur, Santoshpur and Chaipath; Mohanta of Tarakeswar is Mahamandalesvara; the Satis Giri case proved the Daśanāmīs 'Vedic Sannyasis belonging to the school of Sankaracharyya'; 1924 satyagraha; Math declared a public endowment.
quote: Sannyasis belonging to the school of Sankaracharya are Vedic and not Tantric (sic.) Sannyasis, that the Tarakeswar Math is governed by the Sankaracharya school of thought, that the Mohunt of: the Tarakeswar Math...is a Mathadhari Dasanami Sannyasi.
notes: seat=other: a Daśanāmī maṭh tied to Śaṅkara's school by a court ruling, not to a named seat. Not a reprint of BG10 (1912) wording.

institution: Bodh Gaya math of Giri sannyasis (Daśanāmī order 'established by Sankara Acharya')
what_is_said: At the end of the 16th century a Hindu ascetic settled near the ruined temple and founded a maṭh of the Giris, 'one of the seven Saivite orders established by Sankara Acharya'; c. 1727 the Mahanth received the village of Taradih, with the temple ruins, by farman of Muhammad Shah; later disputes with the Buddhists (1890s).
quote: founded a math or monastery of the Hindu sect of Qirs, one of the seven Sai-vite orders established by Sankara Aoharjya.
notes: seat=other: the maṭh itself is not called a Śaṅkara foundation; the Giri order is. Hunter's Gaya (HU12) and the revised Gaya (RV24, 1957) do not repeat the Śaṅkara link for the Bodh Gaya maṭh (RV24 lists 'Sri Mahanth Harihar Gir of Bodh Gaya' among zamindars).

institution: tradition of Śaṅkarācārya and Gaya as a pitṛ-tīrtha
what_is_said: Probably at the end of the 9th century, with the Hindu revival 'due to the efforts of Sankracharya', Gaya was given a place among the five spots of northern India sacred to the manes; also 'a theory that the name Gayawals was given by Shankar'.
quote: It was probably at the end of the ninth century when there was a revival of Hinduism due to the efforts of Sankracharya that Gaya was given a place among the five spots of Northern India sacred to manes
notes: Ādi Śaṅkara tradition only; no institution.

institution: tradition of Śaṅkarācārya's visit to Varanasi
what_is_said: Śaṅkarācārya (c. 8th c.) came from South India to Varanasi to have his monism accepted by the world of scholars (p. 100); even southerners like the great Shankaracharya had to repair to this city (p. 42). No Śaṅkara maṭh in Varanasi is named; maṭhs of Caitanya and Vallabha are.
quote: Shankaracliar)a (circa eighth century A. D.), the great Vedantist philoso- pher, came from South India tO' Varanasi to propound his views and to get his uncompromising monism accepted by the woild of scholaxs
notes: Ādi Śaṅkara (visit tradition). The 1911 Benares volume (UP23 p. 92) only says the restoration of Benares 'began with the itinerant preaching of Shankaracharya'; Atkinson's Benares (AT14 p. 56-57) lists 'Shankaracharya' among Śaiva sects with no maṭh. The Bhinga Dandi Ashram (1924, p. 386) is not linked to a Śaṅkarācārya.

institution: visit of the Sringeri Śaṅkarācārya to Nagpur
what_is_said: 'The successor in office of Sankar Acharya, the spiritual head of the Saivite Hindus of all India, who lives at Sringeri in Madras, visited Nagpur some two or three years ago' (c. 1903-04); the Kalankī Brahmans petitioned him to be allowed to marry other Brahmans and he is believed to have agreed, but no intermarriage has followed.
quote: When the successor in office of Sankar Acharya, the spiritual head of the Saivite Hindus of all India, who lives at Sringeri in Madras, visited Nagpur some two or t hree years ago, it is believed that the KalankI Brahmans submitted a petition to him that they might be allowed to marry
notes: Wardha volume reporting a visit to neighbouring Nagpur. A dated tour of a living Śaṅkarācārya in the Central Provinces.

institution: village named after Śaṅkarācārya's sojourn
what_is_said: Village at the junction of the Hiran and Narmada, 18 miles NE of Narsinghpur; name derived from 'the well-known saint Sankara Charya, who is said to have sojourned here'; fair in Kārttik and Makar Saṅkrānti bathing (c. 5,000).
quote: The name is supposed to be derived from that of the well-known saint Sankara Charya, who is said to have sojourned here.
notes: Ādi Śaṅkara tradition; file is the backup scan in.ernet.dli.2015.206912 of CP06.

institution: local 'shankaracharya' with caste jurisdiction
what_is_said: Brahmans have a dharmādhikārī (hereditary; nine in Basim town alone) and 'a shankaracharya with power to punish for breaches of caste rule'; the shankaracharya 'requires to be personally qualified for his post'.
quote: Brahmans have also a dharmadhikari, who is a final authority on questions of religion, and a shankara- charya with power to punish for breaches of caste rule and the like; the dharmadhtkari holds his office by hereditary right, but should take skilled advice if he is himself unlearned ; there are nine representatives in the single town of Basim ; the shankaracharya requires to be personally qualified for his post
notes: Probably a local deputy of a Śaṅkarācārya (cf. Karvīr/Saṅkeśvar agents in Berar), but no seat named; not a maṭh.

institution: samādhi of a Śaṅkarācārya (Vidyāśaṅkara Bhāratī) and temple of Shankaracharya Swami
what_is_said: Nirmal is sacred for its liṅga and, by tradition, 'the samadhi of one of the great Shankaracharyas'; of eight temples built c. 1750 by Shankraji Keshav (Maratha Subhedar of Vasai) one is dedicated to Shankaracharya Swami, with an annual Government grant, managed by a committee; a week-long fair (c. 6,000 pilgrims from Thane, Raigad, Bombay, Gujarat) on the death anniversary of 'the eighth Shankaracharya Vidyashankar Bharati', Kārttik vadya 11 (p. 1035). s.v. Sopara (p. 1056-57): the great temple of Shankaracharya Swami on Nirmal hill raised by Shankarji Keshav Phadke after the fall of the Portuguese (1739).
quote: according to tradition, the place where stands the samadhi of one of the great Shankaracharyas, the apostle of the modern Brahmanic system.
notes: MISLABELLED FILE: cp/dli.ministry.07863 is the Maharashtra State Gazetteer, Thane District (revised ed., 1982), not CP12 Nagpur 1908. Bombay region; seat not named in the text (the Bombay coder may also meet Nirmal in the 1882 Thana volume). Caste line (Smārt Brahmans refer large questions to the Shankaracharya) counted below.

institution: 'one of the monasteries (Ashram) of Sankaracharya'
what_is_said: Glossary entry: Dwarka, a holy place on the sea in Gujarat, founded by Krishna; 'Site of one of the monasteries (Ashram) of Sankaracharya'.
quote: Site of one of the monasteries (Ash- ram) of Sankaracharya, the founder of the non - dualistic or Vedanta philosophy.
notes: Russell & Hira Lal, Tribes and Castes of the CP vol. I; outside the region, coded only because it is a generic hit in cp/.

institution: Brahman Smārta maṭh of Śaṅkarācārya
what_is_said: Among the chief maṭhs of Tanjore district, alongside the Śūdra (Śaiva) maṭhs of Dharmapuram, Tiruvāvaduturai, Tiruppanandāl and Tiruppagalūr, is the Brahman Smārta maṭh of Śaṅkarācārya at Kumbakonam. Tanjore maṭhs are described in general as endowed, sometimes richly, and as holding the right to appoint priests and managers of rich temples in this and other districts. Fuller account is deferred to ch. XV.
quote: The  chief  of  these  institutions are  the  Sudra  maths  at  Dharmapuram  and  Timv&duturai  in  the M&yavaram  taluk,  at  Tiruppanand&l  (Kumbakdnam  taluk)  and Tiruppagaliir  (Nannilam  taluk)  and  the  Brahman  Smarta  math of  Sankar^cMrya  at  Kumbakonam.
notes: Same text at in.ernet.dli.2015.13345 l.5488 (backup scan). Cross-reference to the Kumbakonam entry (p. 218).

institution: math of Sankaracharya (Smārta)
what_is_said: Important Smārta institution. Said to have been founded in Śaṅkarācārya's own time by a Tanjore king who wished the saint to live in his dominions. Income nearly Rs 14,000 a year. The head appoints the managers of three temples, one of them at Conjeeveram, and nominates his own successor. Library of about 150 books (cadjan, paper MSS and printed) in Telugu and Sanskrit.
quote: There  is  an  important  Sm&rta  religious  institution  here  in  the math  of  SankaracMrya,  which  is  said  to  have  been  founded  in  the time  of  Sankar&ch&rya  himself  by  a Tanjore  king,  who  wished  the saint  to  reside  in  his  dominions.  Its  income  is  nearly  Bs.  14,000 annually,  and  the  head  of  it  appoints  the  managers  of  three temples,  one  of  which  is  at  Oonjeevoram.
notes: The text gives the Kumbakonam seat a founding legend and says nothing about any move from Kāñcī. The Conjeeveram temple is coded separately as a temple link (see S03). Backup scan in.ernet.dli.2015.13345 l.15517.

institution: a temple whose manager is appointed by the head of the Kumbakonam maṭh
what_is_said: The Kumbakonam Śaṅkarācārya maṭh appoints the managers of three temples, one of them at Conjeeveram. The temple is not named (probably Kāmākṣī). The other two temples are not located.
quote: the  head  of  it  appoints  the  managers  of  three temples,  one  of  which  is  at  Oonjeevoram.  He  nominates  his  own successor
notes: Place lies outside the volume's district. The identification of the temple as Kāmākṣī is an inference only; the gazetteer does not name it.

institution: matam founded by Śaṅkarācārya
what_is_said: Śaṅkarācārya (dated 9th or 10th century) paid particular attention to Conjeveram, worked many miracles there and founded a matam or monastery. He is called the founder of the Smārta sect, and the Śaṅkaravijaya is cited. No present-day institution, head, income or estate is described.
quote: He paid particular attention to Conjeveram, where he worked many miracles, and founded a matam, or monastery.
notes: Crole's Manual. The caller gave p. 27; by the OCR page headers the passage is on p. 26, and the Sankara Vijaya sentence runs onto p. 27. The Conjeveram place entry (p. 123–4) mentions Śaṅkara only as the Śaiva reformer whose temples Rāmānuja 'restored'. No maṭh there.

volume: SR08 | Rice, Mysore and Coorg vol II | 1876
institution: matha of a Smārta guru
what_is_said: Agrahāra at the Tunga–Bhadra confluence, 207 houses, population 978, three temples (Brahmeśvara, Narasiṃha, Rāmeśvara). A Smārta guru resides here. The first founder of the maṭha was invested by the Śṛṅgeri svāmi about 500 years ago with authority over the Marāṭhā Brahmans of the sect. The place was plundered and burnt by the Marāṭhā army in 1791.
quote: A guru of the Smartha sect has his residence here. The first founder of the matha was invested by the Shringeri swami, about 500 years ago, with authority to administer to the Mahratta Brahmans of that sect.
notes: The 1876 account says the Marāṭhās put the Śūdra inhabitants to the sword. The 1897 account adds the threat of excommunication.

volume: SR05 | Rice, Mysore gazetteer (1897) vol II | 1897
institution: matha connected with Śṛṅgeri
what_is_said: Sacred village at the confluence, population 949. Seat of a maṭha connected with Śṛṅgeri: the original guru was appointed by the Śṛṅgeri Svāmi about 500 years ago to minister to Smārtas of Marāṭhā descent. A Mādhva maṭha is also there. The Marāṭhās under Paraśurām Bhāu were subject to the Kudali gurus, yet plundered and burnt the place in 1791. They were threatened with excommunication, which they averted by timely gifts. The Śṛṅgeri matha holds a Kadamba copper grant of Śaka 1075 and copper grants of the Keladi chief Somaśekhara Nāyak (17th century) relating to Kudali.
quote: It  is  the  seat  of  a  matha  connected  with  the  one  at  Sring^ri,  the original  Guru  having  been  appointed  by  the  Sring^ri  Swdmi  about  500 years  ago  to  minister  to  the  Smartas  of  Mahratta  descent
notes: A revision of the 1876 text. The copper plates 'the Sring^ri matha has' (p. 460) are probably held at Kudali or bear on it; that is ambiguous, so they are kept in this row. The second scan (mysoreagazettee04ricegoog) is the same text and is not coded separately.

volume: SR05 | Rice, Mysore gazetteer (1897) vol II | 1897
institution: math (guru's establishment) at the foot of Sivaganga hill
what_is_said: Sacred hill called Dakṣiṇa Kāśī. The village at the northern base has population 535. The maṭha is in great financial difficulty, and at the guru's wish the revenues of the religious endowments are being managed by the Muzrai department. The text does not name the maṭha's sect. A Liṅgāyat Rachoṭi maṭh on the eastern face is mentioned separately.
quote: The  math  having  become involved  in  great  pecuniary  difficulties,  the  revenues  of  the  religious endowments  are,  on  the  wish  of  the  giiru,  being  managed  by  the  Muzrai department.
notes: Identification with the Śaṅkara (Smārta) Śivagaṅgā maṭha rests on context only. The math is distinct from the Lingāyat 'Racho?i math' and sits in the village, which matches the Smārta pīṭha. The 1876 vol II (SR08, p. 78–79) has the same Sivaganga entry but no maṭha sentence: it mentions only the Lingayat 'Kachoti math'.

volume: SR08 | Rice, Mysore and Coorg vol II | 1876
institution: residence of a Smārta guru
what_is_said: Avani (319 houses) is a sacred kṣetra associated with Vālmīki, Rāma and Sītā. Its temples were repaired by Yalavanji Rāya and Vāsudeva Rāya, who came from Kumbhakonam with the merchant Navakoṭi Nārāyaṇ Śeṭṭi. A Smārta guru resides here. The Rāmaliṅga festival draws 40,000 people.
quote: Narayan Shetti, from Kmnbhakona, A guru of the Smartha sect resides here.
notes: Seat 'other': Avani (Śṛṅgeri-affiliated Smārta maṭha). The gazetteer does not name the maṭha or its affiliation.

volume: SR05 | Rice, Mysore gazetteer (1897) vol II | 1897
institution: residence of a Smārta guru
what_is_said: Same statement as 1876: a Smārta guru resides at Avani. The temples were repaired in the 14th century by Ilavanji Rāya and Vāsudeva Rāya from Kumbhakona. The festival now draws 10,000 people and 20,000 bullocks.
quote: The  temples  were  repaired  in  the  fourteenth  century  by  Ilavanji Raya  and  Vasudeva  Raya,  who  came,  together  with  a  merchant  named Navakoti^  Narayan  Shetti,  from  Kumbhakona.  A  guru  of  the  Smarta sect  resides  here.
notes: Seat 'other': Avani. Revises the 1876 text.

institution: madam ascribed locally to Śaṅkarācārya
chapter: Places (ch. XV, Ponnāni taluk, s.v. Tānūr)
what_is_said: Near Tānūr the Keraḷādēśapuram temple has an attached Brahman feeding house with inām lands. The madam adjoining the Trikkayikkād temple (said to be founded by Paraśurāma) is locally ascribed to Śrī Śaṅkarācārya. Nothing is said of its present head or endowment.
quote: The latter is a temple founded by Parasu Rama, and the adjoining madam is ascribed locally to Sri Sunkaraeharya.
notes: Innes/Evans. Logan's Manual (1887) has no Śaṅkara maṭha: it mentions only the Keralōlpatti tradition that Śaṅkarācārya laid down the rules for the 72 castes (p. 157) and the Nambūtiris' adoption of his Vedānta (p. 122). Neither gazetteer mentions the Trichur maṭhas (Trichur is in Cochin State).

institution: papal bulls of the Śṛṅgeri Matam concerning the Marka Brahmans
what_is_said: The Marka Brahmans settled at Tali are mostly Kannada Mādhvas, some Smārtas. Other Brahmans do not admit their status, in spite of bulls issued by the Śṛṅgeri Matam (for the Smārtas) and the Parakāla Matam of Mysore (for the Vaiṣṇavas). Source cited: Castes and Tribes I.
quote: In  spite  of  papal  bulla  issued  by  the  SringCri  Matam  on  behalf  of  the Smartas  and  by  the  Parakal  Matam  at  Mysore  on  behalf  of  the  Vaishnavas
notes: Śṛṅgeri exercising jurisdiction over a Smārta group outside Mysore. Not a Places entry, so probably not in sringeri/results/places.tsv. Also in the backup scan in.ernet.dli.2015.61943 l.10117.

institution: guru attending the Hampi festival
chapter: Addenda (note to p. 294, Fairs and festivals)
what_is_said: Mr. Foster explains the falling attendance at the Hampi festival (estimated 100,000 about fifteen years earlier, 60,000 five years earlier, under 40,000 last year): the guru is not allowed to ride into the town, cannot walk, and so declines to come, and the worshippers fall off.
quote: Page 294 — Mr. Foster says of the attendance at the Ilampi festival, “ The reason for the decrease in the number of pilgrims is that the guru is not allowed to ride into the town, and as he cannot walk he declines to come, and the number of worshippers falls off.
notes: The guru is not named. The Virūpākṣa/Hampi Smārta svāmi is the likely referent, since the guru's presence drew the festival crowds, but this is an inference. The main text, p. 294, gives the attendance figures and the sanitary measures. Same addenda probably in the backup scan wbsl.15723, not checked line by line.

institution: Pampāpati (Virūpākṣa) temple additions in honour of Vidyāraṇya; small Vidyāraṇya shrine
chapter: Places (ch. XV, Hospet taluk, s.v. Hampi)
what_is_said: Harihara I made additions to the Pampāpati/Virūpākṣa temple in honour of Mādhava or Vidyāraṇya, the Brahman sage who helped found the city. In ch. II (History) Harihara is said to have built the Pampāpati temple in his honour. A footnote mentions a small shrine to Vidyāraṇya east of the temple, near the Lōkapāvana tank, 'of which the temple Brahmans do not give a clear account'. No maṭha, svāmi or Smārta seat at Hampi is mentioned.
quote: Vijayanagar  chiefs,  in  honour  of  Mddhava  or  Vidyaranya,  the Brahman  sage  who  had  helped  him  in  the  founding  of  the city,*
notes: Scan used: in.ernet.dli.2015.177161 (1916 reprint/backup). The primary scan 207069 has the same text near l.21844. A Vidyāraṇya tradition only. The Virūpākṣa Śaṅkara maṭha (Vidyāraṇya pīṭha) is absent from both Bellary volumes. The 1872 Manual (p. 108) calls Mādhava a disciple of Śaṅkara 'connected with the Sringagiri establishment'; that is not coded.
